title: Songs of Ourselves

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Surprisingly, music is one of the few abilities that all humans have in common. Any individual from Stone Age tribesman to suburban teenager has the ability to recognize and make music without training. Why this should be so is a bit of a mystery. After all, music isn't necessary for survival, language, however, is. With language, members of a tribe can organize a migration across Africa and communicate at night without seeing each other. No other animal has managed to develop this capacity and preference for manipulating symbols and syntax to such a refined extent. Scientists have always been intrigued by the connection between music and language but, over time, words and melody have acquired a vastly different status. Language has long been considered essential to unlocking the mechanisms of man's brainpower. Music, however, is generally treated as a trivial aspect of evolution – mere 'auditory cheesecake,’ as the Harvard cognitive scientist Steven Pinker puts it. However, recent publications suggest that language and music may equally be able to tell us who we are and where we are from – emotionally and biologically.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To grasp the originality of this idea, it's necessary to realize how music has traditionally been understood. First, musicologists have long emphasized that while each country stamps its identity onto music, music itself has some universal qualities. For example, in most countries sound is divided into the 12 intervals that make up the chromatic scale – that is, the scale represented by the keys on the piano. For centuries, observers have attributed this preference for certain combinations of tones to the mathematical properties of sound itself. Some 2,500 years ago, the Greek philosopher Pythagoras noted a direct relationship between the pleasing quality of a tone combination and the physical dimensions of the object producing it. For example, a plucked string plays an octave lower than a similar string half its size. This relation between music and maths is often accompanied by the notion, espoused by Charles Rosen, that music exists apart from the world in which it was created. Painting and sculpture, on the other hand, reproduce at least some aspects of nature, and writing describes familiar thoughts and feelings.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Neither idea is right, according to a recent study carried out by David Schwartz, Catherine Howe and Dale Purves. Human predilections towards music are fundamentally shaped not by elegant algorithms or ratios, but by the messy sounds of real life and of speech, in particular. Schwartz, Howe and Purves analyzed a vast selection of speech sounds to reveal the patterns common to all utterances. Using a database of over 100,000 brief segments of speech, they noted which frequency had the greatest emphasis in each sound and discovered that the resulting frequencies corresponded closely to the chromatic scale. In short, the building blocks of music are to be found in speech. Far from being abstract, music presents a strange analog to the patterns created by the sounds of speech. ‘Music, like the visual arts, is rooted in our experience of the natural world,’ says Schwartz. It emulates our sound environment in the way that visual arts emulate the visual environment. In music, we hear the echo of our basic sound-making instrument – the vocal tract. The explanation for human music is simple: we like the sounds that are familiar to us – specifically, we like the sounds that remind us of us.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Schwartz's study also illuminates the long-running debate as to whether animals understand or enjoy music. Despite the apparent abundance of 'music' in the natural world, previous studies have found that many laboratory animals don't show a great affinity for human music. Marc Hauser and Josh McDermott of Harvard argued in Nature Neuroscience that animals don't create or hear music the way we do. The fact that some laboratory monkeys show awareness of human tunes is evidence, they say, of shared features of the auditory system, not any specific chimpanzee musical ability. As for birds, they generally recognize their own narrow repertoire, but don't generate novel melodies like we do. There are no avian Mozarts. But what has been played to the animals, Schwartz notes, is human music. If animals evolve preferences for sound as we do – based upon the soundscape in which they live – then a cat's idea of a good tune would derive from yowls and meows. To demonstrate that animals don't enjoy sounds the way we do, we'd need evidence that they don't respond to 'music' constructed from their own sound environment. To date we don't have this evidence.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: No matter how the connection between language and music is explained, what is apparent is that our sense of music, even our love for it, is as deeply rooted in our biology and brains as language is. ‘This is most obvious with babies,’ says Sandra Trehub in Nature Neuroscience. For babies, music and speech are on a continuum. Mothers use musical speech to 'regulate infants' emotional states,’ Trehub says. Regardless of what language they speak, the voice all mothers use with babies is the same: 'something between speech and song.’ This kind of interaction ‘puts the baby in a trance-like state, which may proceed to sleep or extended periods of rapture.’ So if the babies of the world could understand the latest research on language and music, they probably wouldn't be very surprised. ‘The upshot,’ says Trehub, ‘is we probably don't realize just how much of a necessity music is.’
